paras: The Winchester circus riot was a street fight between groups of white and Black men in Winchester, Virginia, on the morning of August 29, 1900, while a circus was being unloaded. A white man, William Custy, was knocked unconscious by a Black man named William Pratt, and whites then pursued the fleeing Black men, several of whom were reported severely beaten. Virginia papers called it a "race riot" and "a small race war"; Pratt was later reported arrested.
Sparks' Circus was unloading in Winchester that Wednesday, while the town hosted a state Christian Endeavor convention.

According to a dispatch to the Richmond Times, a white man tried to stop a fight between a white boy and a Black boy, and "a burly negro interfered." A free fight followed, with a number of whites on one side and Black men on the other. Custy, "acting as peace-maker" in the Times account, was knocked unconscious by Pratt.
Believing Custy had been killed, the Black men fled with the whites in pursuit. Custy was "badly hurt," and "several negroes were severely beaten up"; none of the beaten men or the whites were named.

On the day of the riot the Black men were said to have "eluded capture." A week later the Clarke Courier of Berryville reported that Pratt, "Custy's assailant," had fled but "has since been apprehended." No report of charges against any of the whites, or of a trial of Pratt, appears in the coverage.

Only white Virginia papers carried the story, and only as brief items. The Richmond Times put it under the subhead "RACE RIOT" at the end of a convention report; the Alexandria Gazette's shorter version in "Virginia News" stopped at the "free fight." Both centered on the injured white man and the named Black assailant, giving the beating of Black men one clause or none.
The Clarke Courier's follow-up called it "what promised to be a serious riot" and did not mention the beaten Black men. No Black-press coverage of the riot was found.
The two fuller accounts differ on the weapon: the Times said Pratt used brass knuckles, while the Clarke Courier said a black-jack.

reader.title: Winchester circus riot
bases: A street fight between groups of white and Black men ended with whites pursuing the fleeing Black men, several of whom were reported 'severely beaten up' (A2), in what papers called a 'race riot' or 'small race war' (A2, A3).

The Richmond Times dispatch (A2) and the Clarke Courier (A3) independently report the circus-unloading riot and Pratt's attack on Custy; the Alexandria Gazette item (A1) appears to draw on the same dispatch as A2, and only A2 reports the beating of Black men.

accounts.label: Winchester special dispatch to the Richmond Times
accounts.gist: A boys' fight drew in a white man and a 'burly negro', then a free fight between groups; Pratt knocked Custy unconscious with brass knuckles, the Black men fled pursued by whites, and several were severely beaten.

accounts.label: Clarke Courier
accounts.gist: Small boys fighting led to 'a small race war' in which Custy was struck with a black-jack by Pratt, who fled and was later apprehended; no mention of Black men being beaten.

framing.detail: The Times ran the riot under the subhead 'RACE RIOT' inside a convention report, naming the white victim and the Black assailant and noting in one clause that 'several negroes were severely beaten up'.
The Alexandria Gazette and Clarke Courier carried it as a brief among state and local items, the Courier calling it 'what promised to be a serious riot' and 'a small race war'.

conflicts.note: Both name Pratt as the assailant; neither source is clearly better.
Not a true contradiction: A3 is a week later and reports a subsequent arrest.
